claim: When the document carries stamps but the hovered element carries none, say so as its OWN state - the three-state table (disarmed / armed-instrumented / armed-uninstrumented) collapses it into 'armed, instrumented', where it renders identically to 'nothing under the cursor'.
because: ascent's DevInspector implemented all three documented states correctly and still had the failure the technique exists to prevent: hovering a portal or an unstamped module showed 'Hover a component...', the same string as an idle overlay. A fourth state and one line of copy fixed it (502654f9).

claim: When the library/product classifier is an allowlist of repo paths, assert in a test that every entry still resolves on disk - a moved shared root silently reclassifies it as product code and every existing assertion stays green.
because: ascent's LIBRARY_ROOTS carried a comment saying it MUST track layout, and its suite re-typed the same four prefixes rather than reading the list; moving one root in a probe left the suite green until a filesystem guard was added (aa68cbf4).

claim: When a destructive operation has more than one disposition, the receipt must report the one that ran and count every disposition's rows - not just the destructive counter - because the default-safe disposition leaves that counter at zero.
because: ascent's erasure UI read auditDeleted alone while includeAudit:true resolved to redact, so redacting an entire audit trail rendered as '0 rows - audit trail kept'; confirm-by-echo's 'report what was actually destroyed' reads as satisfied by that code. Fixed by reading the response's disposition and summing deleted+redacted, sharing the wording with the preview.

claim: Enumerate a client-boundary type guard by what a client IMPORTS, never by which module path the import came through - an audit scoped to the barrel misses every deep-path import, which is where the richest types usually live.
because: ascent's compile-time wire-safe-date guard listed the 15 client imports from @/lib/db and missed 7 reached via @/lib/db/scans etc., including the entire report trend/diff surface - a third of the real set, unenforced. Widened the audit and the list; all 7 passed, so the gap was in the guard, not the code.

claim: A visibility rule enforced on reads must be enforced on writes in the same terms, and the write refusal should reuse the read's status code - a rule applied to reads alone is a display rule, not an access rule.
because: ascent scoped private org-memory rows on every read path (list, candidates, get-by-id) and on no write; the update was keyed on id alone, so a member who got a 404 READING a colleague's private memory could still overwrite it or flip it to shared. The asymmetry survived review because each layer looked correct alone. Fixed by applying the read's own author test in the write gate, answering 404 rather than 403 so the write path does not disclose existence either.

claim: A debounce and a cancellation answer different questions - the timer stops you issuing a request per keystroke, an abort stops a request you no longer want from landing - so a debounced fetch still needs the abort, or the slower of two in-flight reads wins the setState.
because: two ascent list hooks debounced the timer and fired unguarded fetches; changing a filter twice let the older read overwrite the newer one's rows and its setLoading(false) stop the live spinner. The correct pattern existed three times in the same codebase (including twelve lines below in the same hook), which is evidence the debounce reads as sufficient to authors who know better.

claim: When you ship a GENERATED artifact that executes in a consumer's environment, your own green build is not evidence about it - pin the generated content against the producing repo's own equivalent decision (its runtime pin, its lint config, its command table) so the two cannot drift.
because: ascent pinned Node 24 for itself in .nvmrc, package.json engines and both its workflows while generating node-version: 20 - EOL since April 2026 - into every adopting repo from three separate sites, and a 7,900-test suite stayed green throughout because none of it runs in the consumer's CI. The same blind spot produced a <placeholder> provenance the generated doctor then skipped in silence. Both fixed by deriving the generated value from the producer's own declaration (34691f4d, 0d04f126).

claim: When the standard ships a reference reader, never let it be the only reader in the tests: its parsing model is a SUBSET of the contract, so it is structurally blind to exactly the portability defects the contract exists to prevent.
because: ascent's manifest serializer emitted YAML-ambiguous plain scalars (a repo named `on` produced `name: on`, which a YAML 1.1 parser reads as the boolean true). The suite round-trips the serializer against the shipped zero-dependency doctor field by field - and the doctor treats every value as text, so the one reader in the kit was the one reader that could never detect it. The subject already promises 'an arbitrary tool must be able to read it'; what is missing is that the promise needs a second reader in the test bed to be checkable (562c60e3).

claim: When a contract is split across two authorities that ship in the same repo - a constant declaring identifiers and the elements that must carry them - the comment asserting they cannot drift is the tell that nothing checks. Grep the declared set against the source set; the gap is usually exactly one.
because: ascent's GETTING_STARTED_ANCHORS says 'declared HERE and stamped onto their elements by the UI lane - one shared constant so the model and the DOM can't drift', and 5 of 6 were stamped. The sixth pointed at nothing for as long as it had existed, and the only test asserted step.anchor === ANCHORS[step.id] - the constant against itself, green either way. The technique already asks for a generated manifest plus a gate; what is worth adding is the DIAGNOSTIC: a prose guarantee of non-drift, in a repo where both halves are visible, is a reliable marker for an unenforced contract, and the check costs one grep (bc18bbcd).

claim: When counting 'opened since <start>' over entities that are re-materialized on every snapshot with identity carried across (a scan re-creating every recommendation row), do not read the row's createdAt - diff the identity set of the latest snapshot against the last snapshot strictly before start, seed an EMPTY baseline for every entity that has one, and report 'no pre-window snapshot' as unmeasurable rather than 0.
because: ascent's Recommendation rows are recreated per scan with status carried by (dimId,title); createdAt would have reported every gap on every rescanned repo as opened this week. The identity diff landed in src/lib/db/org-followups-week.ts (fdffc34f); its first draft built the baseline map lazily from rows and silently dropped a repo whose pre-window scan found zero gaps - the test caught it, and the fix (seed a Set per measurable repo) is the half of the rule cohort-matched-comparison does not state.

claim: When one paid operation has two entry points (a JSON route and a streaming twin), put the reserve/refund gate in the shared pre-gate module both routes already call, never inline in one route - the enforcement points must be enumerable from one file.
because: ascent's /api/scan carried six inline credit gates while /api/scan/stream - the only route the report UI actually drives - imported no credit code at all and ran paid LLM inference on private org repos unmetered, under a comment asserting the opposite. Moving the gate into scan-gates.ts (already the declared shared-gates home) closed it for both and shrank the JSON route.

claim: An at-most-once claim marker stored in the audit ledger must be cancelled by appending a signed release record, and the claim reader must treat a marker with a release as not-live - never by deleting the marker, which is the only mutation the ledger will ever grow.
because: ascent's releaseAuditClaim was the sole delete on AuditLog outside retention and erased the evidence that a digest dispatch had been attempted; a sibling table (AlertEvent) had been created specifically to escape that delete. Appending claim.released and widening claimOrgAuditOnce's read kept the at-most-once semantics and the trail.

claim: When a request passes through a per-key limiter and then a global ceiling, check the per-key window first but record the per-key hit only after the global gate admits - a refusal at any later gate must leave the caller's own budget untouched.
because: ascent recorded the per-IP hit before the global check, so during global saturation innocent callers drained their own 20/min budget on requests never served, and the fail-closed body's 'no budget of yours was exceeded' was false. Splitting hit() into checkWindow/recordHit fixed all three paths; three red-then-green tests pin it.

claim: When a tolerant gather stage catches a sensor's failure into the same null or empty value a successful-but-empty read returns, record the failure per sensor and make every downstream rule that would score that value as absence return unknown instead - a caught exception is not a finding about the population.
because: ascent's scan pipeline had fixed this for its PR sensor and left four others (governance, security posture, App inventory, CI health) scoring a thrown fetch as absence; a failed posture read persisted score 0 plus a remediation for a SECURITY.md the org has. A per-sensor failure list threaded into the existing blind-refutation path returned null for the affected checks and one warning named the reads that failed.

claim: When a producer starts excluding a placeholder class (mock scores) from one aggregate, audit every sibling reader that averages, deltas or trends the same rows in the same request - the exclusion is a population rule, not a badge fix, and a half-applied rule produces two fleet numbers on one page.
because: ascent fixed the headline average in one round and the next round's scout found five sibling readers (dimension averages, trend + forecast, movers, team rollup, header chip) still folding mock rows, two of them rendered beside the fixed badge. One exported predicate applied at each reader plus a test per reader closed it.

claim: A recency floor on a per-scan snapshot must be anchored on the snapshot's own present (its newest observed activity), never on the wall clock, or a stale snapshot reads as a fleet nobody works on.
because: ascent's new 90-day enablement floor measured from Date.now() would have emptied 'who to enable next' for any fleet last scanned over a quarter ago; anchoring on the roster's newest lastActiveAt (the same anchor the stale-repo guard already used) kept the cohort honest for stale snapshots.

claim: A gate that exposes policy flags on an unauthenticated surface must announce, per flag, that the flag cannot be evaluated there when its input requires a credential the surface never carries - otherwise the policy echo asserts a bar the verdict never tested and the CLI advertises flags that can never fire.
because: ascent's public gate endpoint always scanned token-less, so three of its advertised bars (branch protection, AI-governed rate, AI authorship) were unconditionally skipped while the body answered pass with requireProtectedBranch: true; a typed skipped[] rendered on all five surfaces plus a structural test keyed on the skip vocabulary closed it.

claim: When one document model feeds several renderers, grep each composed sentence for its caller count: a composer with exactly one caller means the other surfaces are hand-rolling the sentence and will carry the last fix's bug forward.
because: ascent's benchmarkCaption and movementLine each had one caller (the PDF); the tab and the share page rendered the pre-fix wording ('vs 1 repos') that a UAT run had marked resolved after inspecting only the PDF. Routing the HTML through the composers closed the class.

claim: On an agent door, the identity that keys audit actors, per-caller quotas and work-queue leases must be the credential's minted id, never its human-chosen name - names are labels and collide, and a collision on a lease holder is a cross-credential authorization hole.
because: ascent's MCP door keyed the audit actor, the daily write counter and the follow-up claim holder on token:<name>; token names were not unique, so two tokens named ci shared a counter and one could brief and report on the other's leased rows. Keying on the token id with the name as a meta label closed it; a transitional dual-match handles rows written under the old form.

claim: When a decision surface has a write route and a component that renders decisions, grep the route for callers: a decision API with zero product callers means every rendered decision came from a seed or a test, and the honesty machinery around it (re-confirmation, authorship) has never been exercised by a human.
because: ascent's passport decline PATCH had no caller in the product; the hero strip, fleet list, Pareto hollow marks and re-confirmation prompts were all fed by data no owner could enter, and the report-side card had drifted from the fleet list's re-confirm rendering unnoticed. A decline control on the existing PATCH plus a server-stamped author closed it.
